newsitem.title: USA: Clinton heads for sweeping victory.
newsitem.headline: Clinton heads for sweeping victory.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Democratic President Bill Clinton headed for a decisive victory over Republican Bob Dole on Tuesday, sweeping states in the East and the Midwest as polls closed in the U.S. presidential election.

With polls closed in 29 states and the District of Columbia, computerized analysis of voting returns by U.S. television networks projected Clinton taking the vast majority, including the two crucial states of Florida and Ohio.
Dole needed to carry both of these to stand any chance of an upset victory over Clinton, who is bidding to become the first Democrat to win re-election since Franklin Roosevelt in 1936.

Clinton also won the whole of New England, most of the mid-Atlantic seaboard, the Midwest industrial giants of Michigian and Illinois and the potential swing states of Tennessee, New Jersey and Pennsylvania among many others.
Dole was left with Texas, Indiana, Oklahoma, Alabama, South Carolina and his home state of Kansas -- all traditional Republican strongholds.
U.S. elections are actually 51 separate contests in each of the states and the District of Columbia, for votes in the Electoral College, where 270 are needed for victory.
With 21 states left to declare, networks said Clinton had already amassed more than 200 electoral votes and Dole 63. Clinton was expected to reach 270 when more polls closed at 2100 EST (0200 GMT).
Early analysis of the results showed Clinton won largely because of the support of women voters. In Florida, Dole won among men by eight percentage points but Clinton won among women by 16 points.
Voters appeared to have put aside their doubts about Clinton's ethics, giving the president a qualified vote of confidence because of his economic record and compassionate image.
In one exit poll quoted by NBC television, 57 percent of respondents said they did not view Clinton as being honest, against only 43 percent who said he was.
What remained unclear early on was whether Clinton would be able to break the Republican lock on Congress.
But Democratic hopes were raised when the party picked up a Republican Senate seat in New Hampshire and held on to vulnerable seats in Massachusetts, Georgia and New Jersey.

Clinton has made a big effort to gain 50 percent of the total vote, which would enable him to claim the popular mandate he lacked after his 1992 victory, when he was elected with only 43 percent support in a three-way field.
"He's been more moderate, more mainstream, more middle-of-the-road," said Louisiana Democratic Senator John Breaux. "I think he realises that solutions to these problems have to be bipartisan."
Texas billionaire Ross Perot, running for the Reform Party, took 19 percent of the vote four years ago, but fell far short of that mark this time.

Clinton, the 50-year-old Arkansan who is the first president from the post-war "baby-boom" generation, is trying to become the first Democrat re-elected as U.S. president since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944.

Dole, 73, a former Senate majority leader from Kansas and World War II infantryman, was trying to take the presidency back for his generation as well as his party but opinion polls for months have painted him as a prohibitive underdog and views expressed by voters on Tuesday suggested why.
Americas economic prosperity was sure to be a heavy influence on voters and ABC News reported that 58 percent of those leaving the polls rated the U.S. economy in good shape.
That compared with only 19 percent who thought so four years ago, when Clinton ousted Republican President George Bush by hammering at discontent with a weak economy.
NBC said its exit poll also showed that 58 percent believe country is headed in the right direction, compared to two years ago when 60 percent thought it was on the wrong track.

That was when voter discontent with the status quo threw Clinton's Democrats out of Congress by the dozen and turned control of both houses over to the Republican opposition for the first time in 40 years.

The ABC exit poll also suggested Dole's scorching attacks on Clinton's character -- virtually the whole focus of his last two weeks -- gained him little ground among voters who said they cared little about that issue.

Clinton and Dole each concluded the exhausting marathon of their campaigns -- the most expensive and one of the nastiest in U.S. history -- hoarse from brutal last-minute stumping and cast ballots in their respective home bases -- Clinton in Little Rock, Arkansas, and Dole in Russell, Kansas.
An odd quaint sidelight was that, in a nation wired into the computer age and with electronic voting systems, each cast his vote on an old-fashioned paper ballot.
"I've voted before here lots ... but never voted for myself for president. I was a little nervous," Dole said after he and his wife, Elizabeth, left the polling booths.
An ebullient Clinton, seeming more upbeat than Dole, gave his 16-year-old daughter Chelsea a big hug as he emerged from the voting booth in a converted Little Rock train station.

Clinton's polling lead has wavered little all year and the reason was clear: he can point to a country that is prosperous, at peace and without scarring social turmoil. Unemployment is at a seven-year low of 5.2 percent, inflation is only about three percent, stock market indices are sky-high, the federal deficit is barely over one-third what it was when he took office and crime rates are the lowest in a decade.
Against all that, Dole's main promises -- lower taxes and a higher moral tone in the White House -- have not sold.
